questions.q: Which of the following is a real, commonly used way to encode a discrete photonic qubit?
options: The photon's atomic spin quantum number
The photon's rest mass
The electric charge carried by the photon
Polarization, path, or time-bin encoding of a single photon
questions.explain: Discrete photonic qubits commonly encode information in polarization, which path/waveguide a photon travels, or its arrival time slot. Photons have no rest mass and no charge, so those can't carry qubit information.

questions.q: Why can photonic quantum computers operate at or near room temperature, unlike superconducting qubits?
options: Room temperature operation was only achieved very recently and doesn't apply to most photonic hardware
Photonic circuits use a special material that is immune to all forms of heat
Photons are heavier than electrons and therefore less affected by temperature
Photons don't interact with their thermal environment the way charge-based or spin-based qubits do, so there's no need for a dilution refrigerator
questions.explain: Photons don't couple to thermal noise in the way superconducting circuits or trapped charges do, which is why photonic hardware avoids the extreme cooling requirements of other modalities -- a genuine structural advantage.

questions.q: What role do beamsplitters and phase shifters play in a photonic quantum computer?
options: They are linear optical elements used to perform single-qubit operations
They are used exclusively to cool the photonic chip to millikelvin temperatures
They permanently store photons between computations
They convert photons into superconducting qubits for processing
questions.explain: Beamsplitters (mixing optical paths) and phase shifters (delaying one path relative to another) are linear optical elements that implement single-qubit gates. They don't cool, store, or convert photons into another qubit type.

questions.q: Why is 'heralding' used in some linear-optical approaches to two-photon entangling gates?
options: Because it eliminates the need for any optical nonlinearity in the circuit
Because heralding permanently fixes photon loss so it never happens again
Because it is required to encode information in a photon's polarization
Because those two-photon gates succeed only probabilistically, and an auxiliary detection event is needed to confirm (herald) that a given attempt actually worked
questions.explain: Photons don't naturally interact strongly, so some two-photon gate schemes succeed only some of the time; heralding uses an extra measurement to signal success so failed attempts can be identified and retried.

questions.q: Why is photon loss considered the dominant, and especially hard to correct, error source in photonic quantum computing?
options: Photons cannot be lost once they enter a photonic integrated circuit
Photon loss is actually easier to correct than any other error type in any quantum hardware platform

A lost photon is simply gone -- unlike a decohering trapped ion or superconducting qubit that is still physically present and can potentially be measured or corrected, there is no equivalent way to recover a photon that's been absorbed, scattered, or missed by a detector
Photon loss only affects continuous-variable encodings and never affects discrete photonic qubits
questions.explain: Because the photon is the physical carrier and travels at light speed with no way to 'pause' or re-measure it in place, once it's absorbed, scattered, or mis-detected it is unrecoverable -- a fundamentally different problem from decoherence in a stationary qubit.
